title: The table, many views
hook: Mass, Divine Liturgy, Lord's Supper: Catholics and Orthodox say Christ is truly present; many Protestants say spiritually, or by remembrance

segments.voice: Yesterday: baptism, for infants in many churches and for choosing believers in others. Your line was you were named. Did you hear your name differently? Day one hundred fifty-three.

This Sunday, all over the world, something is happening that has happened every week for nearly two thousand years. In a Catholic cathedral, a priest lifts a round white host while a bell rings. In an Orthodox church, a spoon of bread soaked in wine is placed on a child's tongue. In a Baptist church, trays of tiny cups of grape juice are passed down the pews. In a Lutheran church, people kneel at a rail. It has different names, Mass, the Divine Liturgy, the Lord's Supper, Holy Communion, and Christians understand it in genuinely different ways. But everyone is doing what Jesus did the night before he died. And one of its oldest names is a word you already know, if you speak Greek.
screen: `A HOST LIFTED, A BELL RINGS.` → `A SPOON, TRAYS OF CUPS, A RAIL.` → `THE SAME NIGHT, REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Eucharist. From the Greek eucharistia: thanksgiving. Eu, good. Charis, grace, gift. Walk into a café in Athens today and say efcharistó, and you've just said thank you. The oldest account of the last supper in the Bible is from Paul, writing to Corinth, and here's what he says Jesus did, in the King James Bible: "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me." Given thanks: that's the verb, eucharisteō. The whole meal is named for the thank you. Now, what happens at that table? Here, churches differ, and they hold their views in earnest. Catholics believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood, while still looking like bread and wine; they call this transubstantiation. Orthodox Christians also say Christ is truly present, and prefer to call it a holy mystery rather than explain how. Lutherans say Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many Reformed and Presbyterian Christians say Christ is truly present, but spiritually, received by faith. And many Baptists and others see the meal as a memorial, a powerful act of remembering what Jesus did, as he said: do this in remembrance of me. Anglicans hold a range of these views within one church. How often varies too: daily Mass for some Catholics, weekly for many churches, monthly or quarterly for others. Under the disagreement sits something every one of these churches would say: this meal begins with gratitude. Before anything else, Jesus gave thanks.
screen: `EUCHARISTIA — THANKSGIVING.` · `WHEN HE HAD GIVEN THANKS, HE BRAKE IT.` · `TRULY PRESENT, SPIRITUAL, OR MEMORIAL.` · `IT BEGINS WITH GRATITUDE.` · then, large: `THIS DO IN REMEMBRANCE OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you have a piece of bread, or a cracker, or anything simple to eat, hold it. If not, imagine one. This isn't communion. Just an ordinary meal, eaten slowly. Look at it. Think of the wheat, the field, the baker, the hands it passed through to reach you. Say thank you, in whatever way you say it. Then take one small bite, and eat it slowly, tasting it. If you pray, you can give thanks to God. If you don't, give thanks to everyone who brought it to you. The bell holds the time.
Eucharist. Greek for thanksgiving. The Lord's Supper, named for the thanks Jesus gave before he broke the bread.
Your line: thanksgiving. Today, before one meal, pause and give thanks, then eat the first bite slowly. Day one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Christians share the Eucharist, also called Mass, the Divine Liturgy, the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion, with bread and wine or grape juice; Catholics and Orthodox usually receive weekly or more, while some Protestant churches share it monthly or quarterly.

fork.setup: it's the night before he dies. Jesus takes the bread. what does he do first?
fork.reveal: "when he had given thanks, he brake it." the verb is eucharisteō, and the whole meal came to be named for that thank you.

original.note: Greek: thanksgiving — eu, good, and charis, grace or gift.

trapdoor: what you thought: Eucharist is a churchy word for communion.
what it means: thanksgiving, the meal named for Jesus's thanks, understood by churches as real presence, spiritual presence or memorial.
what a scholar hears: eucharisteō in 1 Corinthians 11:24, probably the earliest written account of the supper, from the 50s.

notes: Summary of views: Catholic transubstantiation; Orthodox real presence as mystery; Lutheran sacramental union ('in, with and under'); Reformed spiritual real presence; Baptist/Zwinglian memorial; Anglican range. Please confirm each is fairly and neutrally described.
Modern Greek ευχαριστώ (efcharistó) = thank you. Confirm.
1 Corinthians dated c. 53–55 and generally held to predate the written gospels. Confirm.
Orthodox communion by spoon of bread in wine: confirm.
Practice is explicitly 'not communion' to avoid imitating a sacrament.
